title: Organs of the digestive tract (anterior)
attribution: 3D anatomy from Z-Anatomy, built on BodyParts3D (CC BY-SA). Rendered in Blender; surface detail added with an image model.

rows: Right upper part of the abdomen, under the diaphragm and mostly under cover of the ribs.
Processes nutrients, makes bile, plasma proteins and clotting factors, stores glycogen, and clears drugs and toxins from the blood.
Two sources: the hepatic portal vein, which brings most of the blood, and the proper hepatic artery. The hepatic veins drain it into the inferior vena cava.
hy: The portal triad (bile duct, proper hepatic artery, portal vein) runs in the hepatoduodenal ligament; squeezing it there (Pringle maneuver) controls bleeding from the liver.

rows: Upper left part of the abdomen, between the esophagus and the duodenum.
Stores and churns food. Its parietal cells secrete acid and intrinsic factor and its chief cells secrete pepsinogen.
All from the celiac trunk: left and right gastric arteries along the lesser curvature, left and right gastro-omental arteries along the greater curvature, and short gastric arteries to the fundus.
hy: Without intrinsic factor (pernicious anemia, or after removal of the stomach) vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed.

rows: In a fossa on the lower surface of the liver. Its fundus reaches the edge of the liver at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage.
Stores and concentrates bile and releases it into the duodenum when cholecystokinin makes it contract.
Cystic artery, usually a branch of the right hepatic artery.
hy: In acute cholecystitis, pressing under the right ribs stops the patient from breathing in (Murphy sign), and the pain may be felt in the right shoulder.

rows: Lies across the back wall of the abdomen behind the stomach. Its head sits in the curve of the duodenum and its tail reaches the spleen.
Exocrine part: digestive enzymes and bicarbonate, released into the duodenum. Endocrine part (islets): insulin, glucagon and somatostatin.
hy: A cancer of the head of the pancreas blocks the bile duct and causes painless jaundice, often with a gallbladder that can be felt (Courvoisier sign).

rows: Runs from the pharynx at C6 down through the chest, behind the trachea and the left atrium, and through the diaphragm at T10 to the stomach.
Carries food to the stomach by waves of contraction. Its upper third is striated muscle and its lower third smooth muscle.
hy: Its lower end is a portosystemic anastomosis, where esophageal varices form in portal hypertension.
Long-standing acid reflux changes the lining of its lower end to intestinal-type epithelium (Barrett esophagus), which can turn into adenocarcinoma.

rows: Coils in the central and lower abdomen, hung from the back wall by the mesentery, from the end of the duodenum to the cecum.
Completes digestion and absorbs nutrients. The last part of the ileum absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts.
Jejunal and ileal branches of the superior mesenteric artery.
hy: A Meckel diverticulum, a remnant of the vitelline duct, lies on the ileum about 2 feet from the cecum, occurs in about 2% of people and can bleed because it may contain stomach lining.

rows: Right side of the abdomen, from the cecum up to the right colic (hepatic) flexure. It is fixed to the back wall of the abdomen.
Absorbs water and salts from the contents of the gut.
Ileocolic and right colic branches of the superior mesenteric artery.
Crosses the upper abdomen from the right colic flexure to the left colic flexure, hanging on its own mesentery.
Absorbs water and salts from the contents of the gut.
Middle colic branch of the superior mesenteric artery for its first two thirds; left colic branch of the inferior mesenteric artery for its last third.
hy: The splenic flexure, where it ends, lies at the border between the superior and inferior mesenteric territories and is the part of the colon most at risk of ischemia when blood pressure falls.

rows: Left side of the abdomen, from the left colic (splenic) flexure down to the sigmoid colon. It is fixed to the back wall of the abdomen.
Left colic branch of the inferior mesenteric artery.
S-shaped loop in the lower left abdomen and pelvis, between the descending colon and the rectum, on its own mesentery.
Stores feces until they pass into the rectum.
Sigmoid branches of the inferior mesenteric artery.
hy: The most common site of diverticula of the colon and of diverticulitis, which causes pain in the lower left abdomen.
Its long mesentery lets it twist on itself (sigmoid volvulus), especially in older adults.

rows: Upper left part of the abdomen, against the diaphragm and under ribs 9 to 11.
Filters the blood, removes old red cells and bacteria, and takes part in immune responses.
Splenic artery, a branch of the celiac trunk. The splenic vein drains into the hepatic portal vein.
hy: After removal of the spleen there is a lasting risk of severe infection with encapsulated bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis).
It is often injured in blunt trauma to the left lower ribs, and bleeding from it can cause pain in the left shoulder (Kehr sign).
